passage:
Monday. Jahnavi and Rafiq both showed Ma their drawings. Ma used to say whose was better. This time she said, "Jahnavi, you worked so long on the shading. Rafiq, look how brave those colours are." Both grinned.
Wednesday. They argued over the swing. Ma stayed at the window, watching, and did not step in. After some shouting, Rafiq said, "Five pushes each?" Jahnavi agreed.
Saturday. Rafiq climbed too high on the wall. Ma came out at once and helped him down. Later, when Jahnavi's kite tangled, Rafiq helped her fix it without anyone asking. Ma noticed they hadn't said "I'm better" all week.

qa.q: What deal did Rafiq suggest for the swing?
What does Rafiq helping with the kite unasked suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt at ease rather than in competition with Jahnavi, so he was willing to help her now that he isn't being compared.

qa.q: What did Ma do differently that helped?
qa.a: She praised each child's own effort, let them solve the swing quarrel themselves and stepped in only when Rafiq was unsafe on the wall.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi experience her mother's new way of praising?
qa.a: Jahnavi likely feels seen for their own work, like the shading, so there is no need to beat Rafiq to feel good.

grounding: It shows a parent praising each child's own effort, letting them settle small quarrels and stepping in only for safety, easing rivalry.

passage: Vaibhav, you asked your Indu Dadi why I never say which of you cousins is the cleverest. Sit, I'll tell you. When your Papa and his brother were small, I always compared. "Look at Suresh's marks, why can't you?" They fought all the time, over everything. One day a teacher told me, "Praise each one for what he does." So I tried. I told your Papa his handwriting was careful, and Suresh that he was a good runner. When they quarrelled over small things, I let them sort it out, and only stepped in if someone might get hurt. Slowly, they stopped trying to beat each other. Now they talk every day.

qa.q: What did Indu Dadi praise Vaibhav's Papa for?
How did Indu Dadi feel about her old habit of comparing?
qa.a: She seems to regret it, since it made her sons fight over everything, which is why she changed.

qa.q: What approach did Indu Dadi switch to, and why did it work?
qa.a: She praised each son for his own strengths and let them solve small quarrels, so they no longer had to compete for her approval.

qa.q: How might Suresh have felt when his mother stopped comparing?
qa.a: He probably felt less pressure and more valued for his running, and less need to beat his brother.

grounding: It illustrates a parent who stops comparing, praises each child's own strengths and lets small quarrels be settled by them, so the siblings stop competing.
